title: Adaptation: why a fish has fins and a camel has a hump

summary.text: A fish has fins, gills and a small bag of air inside her. A camel has a hump of fat, wide feet and long eyelashes. Each of these body parts helps with a problem of their own place: water all around, or hot, dry sand. A body part like this is called an adaptation. Your child makes a bottle fish with coins inside, and finds that a few spoons of air are enough to stop it sinking. You also look at plants suited to dry places and wet places, and at humans, who are animals suited to places too.
summary.art: A split picture: on the left a silver fish swimming in blue water with her fins spread, on the right a camel walking on orange sand dunes, and a girl in the middle holding a plastic bottle with coins inside.

intro.hook: A fish cannot breathe for long on hot sand. A camel cannot breathe under water. Why is each of them so good at living in one place, and so bad at the other?
intro.text: Look at a fish and a camel side by side. The fish has flat fins, a smooth body and gills on the sides of her head. The camel has a hump, long legs, wide soft feet and very long eyelashes. Nothing about the fish would help on sand, and nothing about the camel would help under water. In this unit you find out what each body part does, and you make a bottle fish to test how a fish stays up in the water.
intro.art: A fish and a camel drawn side by side on a notebook page, with arrows pointing to the fish's fins and gills and to the camel's hump, feet and eyelashes.

outcomes: By the end I can say what an adaptation is, and give an example of a body part that suits a place.
By the end I can explain how fins, gills and a swim bladder help a fish live in water.
By the end I can explain how a camel's hump, feet, eyelashes and fur help her in the desert, and say that the hump is fat, not water.
By the end I can show with my bottle fish that a little air stops a heavy body from sinking.
By the end I can name a plant suited to a dry place and a plant suited to a wet place, and say one way each one is suited.
By the end I can say that adaptations pass from parents to their young over many generations, and that humans are animals suited to places too.

terms.meaning: A habitat is the place where a living being lives and finds what they need.
terms.example: A pond is a habitat for fish and frogs. The Thar Desert is a habitat for camels.
terms.art: A pond with lotus leaves and a fish under the water, next to a small picture of sand dunes with a camel.

terms.meaning: An adaptation is a body part, or a way of behaving, that helps a living being live in their habitat.
terms.example: A camel's wide feet are an adaptation for walking on soft sand.
terms.art: A camel's wide, flat foot pressing on sand, with a small sinking shoe next to it for comparison.

terms.meaning: A fin is a thin, flat part that sticks out of a fish's body. Fins push on the water, steer and keep the fish upright.
terms.example: A fish's tail fin pushes her forward. The fins on her sides help her turn and stop.
terms.art: A side view of a rohu fish with each fin coloured differently.

terms.meaning: Gills are the parts a fish breathes with. They take oxygen out of the water.
terms.example: If you lift the flap behind a fish's eye at the market, you see the red gills.
terms.art: A close-up of a fish's head with the gill flap lifted, showing feathery red gills.

terms.meaning: A swim bladder is a small bag of gas inside many fish. It stops the fish from sinking.
terms.example: A goldfish can stay still in the middle of her tank because of her swim bladder.
terms.art: A see-through drawing of a fish with a pale balloon-shaped swim bladder inside her belly.

terms.meaning: A camel's hump is a big lump of fat on her back. Fat is stored food.
terms.example: When a camel has had little food for a long time, her hump gets smaller.
terms.art: Two camels side by side: one with a tall, firm hump and one with a small hump flopping to one side.

terms.meaning: A desert is a place that gets very little rain.
terms.example: The Thar Desert in Rajasthan is hot in the day and can be cold at night.
terms.art: Sand dunes of the Thar at sunset with a few thorny bushes.

terms.meaning: A spine on a cactus is a hard, sharp point. A cactus's spines are leaves that have changed shape.
terms.example: A cactus on a balcony has spines in place of flat green leaves.
terms.art: A close-up of a green cactus stem with clusters of thin white spines.

terms.meaning: Something floats when the water holds it up at the top. It sinks when it goes down to the bottom.
terms.example: An empty bottle with the cap on floats. A steel spoon sinks.
terms.art: A bucket of water with a floating bottle at the top and a steel spoon lying at the bottom.

terms.meaning: A generation is one step in a family: grandparents, then parents, then children.
terms.example: A camel calf, her mother and her grandmother are three generations of camels.
terms.art: A camel calf, her mother and her grandmother standing in a row on sand, in three sizes.

explanations.context: This card says what the word adaptation means.
explanations.definition: An adaptation is a body part, or a way of behaving, that helps a living being live in their habitat.
explanations.description: Every habitat has its own problems. In water, a body must move, breathe and stay up. In a desert, a body must save water and walk on hot sand. A living being's adaptations are their answers to these problems. An adaptation that helps in one place may be no help in another. Wide feet help a camel on sand, but they would not help a fish.
examples: A fish's fins help her swim.
A camel's long eyelashes keep sand out of her eyes.
A lotus leaf floats on a pond.
Your sweat cools you on a hot day.
explanations.art: Four small boxes: a fish's fin, a camel's eyelashes, a floating lotus leaf, and a child's forehead with drops of sweat.

explanations.concept: Fins: how a fish moves in water
explanations.context: This card is about the fins of a fish, and what each one does.
explanations.definition: Fins are thin, flat parts of a fish's body that push on the water.
explanations.description: A fish swims by bending her body from side to side. Her tail fin pushes the water back, and the water pushes her forward. The fin on her back stops her from rolling over. The fins on her sides help her steer, turn and stop. Water is thick and heavy to move through, so a fish's body is smooth and narrow at the front. Her slime protects her skin from germs.
examples: A rohu has seven fins.
A sardine, called mathi in Kerala, swims fast with her forked tail fin.
A pomfret is flat and tall, and turns quickly between rocks.
explanations.art: A fish seen from the side and from above, with arrows showing the tail fin pushing water back and the fish moving forward.

explanations.context: This card is about how a fish breathes under water, and how she stays up without sinking.
explanations.definition: Gills take oxygen out of water. A swim bladder is a bag of gas inside many fish that stops them sinking.
explanations.description: Water has a little oxygen mixed into it. A fish's gills are many thin red flaps. In water the flaps spread apart and take oxygen into her blood. Out of water, they stick together and dry out, so most fish cannot breathe for long in air. A fish's bones and muscles are a little heavier than water. Many fish carry a swim bladder, a bag of gas inside, so the whole fish weighs the same as the water around her and stays at one depth. Sharks have no swim bladder, and many sharks slowly sink if they stop swimming.
examples: A goldfish hangs still in her tank.
A carp gulps air at the top of a pond to fill her swim bladder.
A shark keeps swimming, or sinks slowly to the sea floor.
explanations.art: A see-through fish showing red gills behind her head and a pale swim bladder in her belly, hanging still in the middle of the water.

explanations.concept: A camel's body for the desert
explanations.context: This card is about the parts of a camel's body that help her in the desert.
explanations.definition: A camel's hump, feet, eyelashes, nostrils and fur are adaptations to hot, dry, sandy places.
explanations.description: The camels of the Thar Desert have one hump. The hump is a store of fat, not water. When food is hard to find, the camel lives on this fat, and the hump gets smaller. Her feet are wide, with two toes joined by a soft, thick pad that spreads out on sand. Two rows of long eyelashes, and a thin third eyelid, keep sand out of her eyes. She can close her nostrils to thin slits in a sandstorm. Thick fur on her back keeps the sun's heat off her skin. Hard, thick pads of skin on her knees and chest let her kneel on hot sand.
examples: A camel at the Pushkar fair in Rajasthan kneels on her chest pads to rest.
Bactrian camels, with two humps, live in the cold Nubra Valley of Ladakh.
A camel can eat thorny babool and khejri branches without hurting her mouth.
explanations.art: A camel with labels pointing to her hump, long eyelashes, slit nostrils, thick back fur, knee pads and wide feet.

explanations.concept: Why is a camel's fat in one hump?
explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists have ideas about, but cannot test easily.
explanations.description: Most animals store fat as a layer under the skin, all over the body. A camel keeps much of hers in one hump. Nobody can be completely sure why. The main idea is about heat. A layer of fat all over would act like a blanket and keep heat in. With the fat in one place, heat can leave the rest of her body more easily.
examples: A buffalo stores fat all over her body.
A camel stores much of her fat in her hump.

perspectives.explanation: Keeping fat in one hump lets heat escape from the rest of the camel's body, which helps in a hot desert.
The hump may simply be the best place to carry a big food store while walking long distances. The heat idea may be only part of the answer.

explanations.art: Two outline drawings: a buffalo with a thin fat layer shaded all round her body, and a camel with the fat shaded only in her hump, with wavy heat lines leaving her sides.

explanations.context: This card is about plants that are suited to very dry places and very wet places.
explanations.definition: Plants have adaptations too: in their leaves, stems, roots and seeds.
explanations.description: Plants lose water through their leaves, so many plants of dry places have tiny leaves, or none at all. A cactus has spines in place of leaves, and stores water in her thick, waxy green stem. An aloe keeps water in thick, juicy leaves, and opens the tiny holes in her leaves at night, when the air is cool. In a pond, a lotus leaf floats, and rain rolls off her waxy top. Mangrove trees grow in salty mud by the sea, and push breathing roots up out of the mud to get air. A coconut floats on the sea for weeks, and can grow on a new beach far away.
examples: A cactus on a balcony in Chennai.
The ker bush of the Thar, who has almost no leaves and makes food in her green stems.
Lotus leaves in a temple tank.
Mangrove roots at Pichavaram in Tamil Nadu and in the Sundarbans.
Khejri trees in the Thar, with very deep roots.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study what plants sense
perspectives.explanation: Plants sense their world and decide what to do. An aloe senses the cool of the night and opens her leaf holes then, to save water.
These are automatic responses, built into the plant's cells, with no thinking needed.

explanations.art: A row of four plants: a cactus with spines, an aloe with thick leaves, a lotus leaf floating on water with rain drops rolling off, and a mangrove with breathing roots sticking up out of mud.

explanations.context: This card is about how living beings come to have their adaptations.
explanations.definition: Adaptations pass from parents to their young, and change slowly over very many generations.
explanations.description: A camel calf is born with wide feet and long eyelashes, before she has ever walked on sand. She got them from her parents. In every family, some young are a little different from others. In a desert, young camels whose feet spread a little wider might walk more easily and live longer. They have more calves, who are born with wide feet too. Over thousands of generations, the whole family changes to suit their place. One camel cannot grow wider feet by walking on sand, and pass them on.
examples: A puppy has her mother's ears.
A camel calf has long eyelashes at birth.
A baby fish hatches with fins.
explanations.art: A mother camel and her calf walking on sand, both with wide feet, and a faint row of older camels stretching back behind them.

explanations.concept: Humans are animals suited to places too
explanations.context: This card is about the adaptations of people, who are animals like all the others.
explanations.definition: Humans have adaptations to their habitats, just like other animals.
explanations.description: Humans cool down by sweating. Our skin has millions of tiny sweat glands, and sweat drying on the skin carries heat away. Some groups of people have adaptations to their own places. The Bajau people of Indonesia have dived for fish for over a thousand years. In 2018, the scientist Melissa Ilardo found that their spleens are bigger than those of their neighbours. The spleen is an organ that stores blood, and a bigger one may help them dive for longer. Tibetan people live high in the mountains, where the air is thin. In 2014, Emilia Huerta-Sánchez and her team found a small difference in their genes, the instructions passed from parents to children, that helps them live there. People also suit themselves to places by what they make: boats, shawls and houses.
examples: You sweat when you run on a hot day.
Bajau divers can stay under water for a long time.
Tibetan people live well in thin mountain air.
explanations.art: A child running and sweating on a hot day, a Bajau diver swimming under the sea, and a Tibetan woman walking in high mountains.

agreed.text: Fish breathe with gills, which take oxygen out of the water.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have watched water flow in through a fish's mouth and out over the gills. The blood leaving the gills carries more oxygen than the blood going in.

agreed.text: A camel's hump is a store of fat, not water.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have measured what the hump is made of. When a camel has little food for a long time, the hump shrinks and can flop to one side.

agreed.text: Adaptations pass from parents to their young, and change over many generations.
agreed.evidence: Young animals are born with the adaptations of their family. A camel calf has wide feet and long eyelashes before she ever walks on sand.

agreed.text: Fish, camels and humans all come from the same ancient ancestors.
agreed.evidence: Fossils show fish with fin bones that slowly became the leg bones of four-legged animals. Your arm has the same pattern of bones.

challenging.claim: A camel's hump is full of water.
challenging.who: A very common idea in many countries
challenging.for: Camels can go many days without drinking, so people guessed they carried water.
challenging.against: The hump is mostly fat. When a camel has no food for a long time, her hump gets smaller and can flop to one side.
challenging.context: This card is about a mistake many people still make.

challenging.claim: Every fish dies quickly out of water.
challenging.for: Most fish cannot breathe for long in air, because their gills stick together and dry out.
challenging.against: Mudskippers in mangroves hop about on mud, breathing through their skin and the inside of their mouth. The climbing perch, called koi in Bengal, breathes air with a special organ and can wriggle across wet ground.
challenging.context: This card is about fish who can live out of water for a while.

challenging.claim: Legs first grew so that fish could walk on land.
challenging.who: Many scientists in the 1900s, such as Alfred Romer in America
challenging.for: Some fish living in drying ponds might have used strong fins to crawl to the next pond.
challenging.against: In 1987, Jenny Clack's team found Acanthostega, an animal with legs who also had gills and a tail fin, and lived in water. So legs first helped in water.
challenging.context: This card is about where the first legs were used.

challenging.claim: Fingers wrinkle in water to help us grip wet things.
challenging.who: Mark Changizi and other scientists, from 2011
challenging.for: In a test in 2013, people with wrinkled fingers moved wet marbles faster than people with smooth fingers.
challenging.against: In another test in 2014, wrinkled fingers did not help at all. Scientists still argue about it.
challenging.context: This card is about a question you can test yourself.

big_questions.q: Your bottle fish needed only a little air to float. Why is air so light?
big_questions.hint: Squeeze an empty bottle with the cap off. The air rushes out easily. What does that tell you about air?

big_questions.q: A fish lives in water all her life. Does she notice that she is wet?
big_questions.hint: Air is all around you all day. When do you notice it?

big_questions.q: Is any place on Earth a bad place to live, or only a bad place for some bodies?
big_questions.hint: Think of the camel in the sea and the fish in the desert. Then think of the mudskipper.

big_questions.q: Why does a cactus have spines, but a lotus has wide, soft leaves?
big_questions.hint: Think about how much water each plant can get, and how leaves lose water.

big_questions.q: If people lived on the Moon for a thousand years, would their bodies change?
big_questions.hint: Adaptations change over many generations. What would be different for a body on the Moon?

story.title: Moti and the Mathi
story.note: A made-up story. Camels really do have humps of fat, thick fur that keeps out the sun's heat, nostrils that close in sandstorms, two rows of eyelashes, wide padded feet and hard pads for kneeling.
text: Anju lived in Kochi, near the backwaters. She was seven, and she knew a lot about fish.
Every Sunday she went to the fish market with her grandmother, Ammamma. Ammamma had sold fish there for forty years. Anju knew the silver mathi, the striped bangda and the flat, shining pomfret.
One December, Anju's Amma went to work for two weeks at a children's health camp. The camp was in Jaisalmer, in the Thar Desert in Rajasthan. Amma was a doctor. Anju and her Appa went with her.

The desert was nothing like Kochi. There were no backwaters, no coconut trees and almost no green. There was sand in long, soft hills, and thorny bushes, and a huge blue sky. The mornings were cold, so cold that Anju wore a shawl. By noon the sun was hot on her head.
On the second day, they met Bhanwari. Bhanwari kept camels at the edge of the village. Her favourite camel was called Moti. Moti was tall and sandy brown, with one big hump.
'Poor Moti,' said Appa. 'Look at all that thick fur in this heat. Someone should cut it short for her.'
Bhanwari laughed. 'Wait until noon,' she said, 'then put your hand on her back.'
At noon Anju put her hand flat on Moti's back. The top of the fur was hot from the sun. Then she pushed her fingers deep into the fur, down near the skin. It was much cooler there.
'The fur keeps the sun's heat off her skin,' said Bhanwari. 'And tonight, when it is cold, it will keep her warm.'
Appa nodded slowly. 'And that hump is her water tank,' he said. 'That is how she goes days without drinking.'

'Many people think so,' said Bhanwari. 'But it is fat. When there is no good food, Moti lives on her fat. Then the hump gets smaller and flops over to one side. When she eats well again, it fills up.'
Anju wrote it all down in her notebook. HUMP: FAT, NOT WATER. FUR: KEEPS THE SUN OUT.
That afternoon a strong wind blew. Sand flew through the air and stung Anju's legs. She shut her eyes tight and coughed. Moti did not seem to mind at all. Bhanwari pointed at the camel's face.
'Look at her nose,' she said. Moti had squeezed her nostrils into two thin slits. Her eyes were half shut behind two rows of long eyelashes.
'She has eyelashes like a film star,' said Anju, and Bhanwari laughed again.

When the wind dropped, they walked out on the dunes. Appa's shoes sank deep into the soft sand with every step. He puffed and slipped. Moti walked beside him easily. Anju watched her big, round feet. Each foot spread out wide and flat as it pressed on the sand.
'Her feet are like two chapatis,' said Anju.

Then Moti folded her front legs and knelt on the hot sand. Under her chest and on her knees there were thick, hard pads of skin, like the heel of a foot. 'She can kneel anywhere,' said Bhanwari, 'even on sand that would burn your hand.'

Two weeks later, Anju was back in Kochi. On Sunday she went to the fish market with Ammamma. She picked up a mathi and looked at the fish carefully. The mathi had no hump, no eyelashes and no feet. She was smooth and slippery, with a forked tail fin and small fins on her sides. Ammamma lifted the flap behind the eye. The gills underneath were bright red.
'Ammamma,' said Anju, 'why doesn't a fish have a hump?'
Ammamma smiled. 'What would a fish do with a hump in the sea?' she asked.

Anju thought about it. The sea is full of water, so a fish never needs to save any. The water holds a fish up, so she does not need wide feet. She needs fins to push the water and to steer. She needs gills to take oxygen out of the water.
'And Moti needs a hump for the days with no food,' said Anju. 'And wide feet for the sand. And eyelashes for the wind.'
She thought of Moti standing in the backwaters, sinking into the mud. Then she thought of the mathi lying on a hot dune. She laughed.
'Moti would be no good here,' she said. 'And the mathi would be no good there. Each one is made for her own place.'
That night she drew Moti and the mathi side by side in her notebook. Under Moti she wrote: MADE FOR SAND. Under the mathi she wrote: MADE FOR WATER.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Anju compares two animals from two very different places. She sees that every part of the camel answers a problem of the desert, and every part of the fish answers a problem of the water. Each body suits their own place, and would be no help in the other.
ask: Why did Appa think Moti's fur was a bad idea? What did Anju find when she felt the fur?
What did Bhanwari say the hump is for?
Why doesn't a fish need a hump?

games.title: Who Am I? A three-clue guessing game
games.context: This is a guessing game about living beings and their adaptations. Each card gives three clues, one at a time. The fewer clues you need, the more points you win.

printables.title: 12 clue cards to cut out, with the answer on the back

items.f: 1. I have fins and gills. 2. I live in ponds in Bengal and Assam. 3. I can breathe air, and I can wriggle across wet ground.
items.b: The climbing perch, called koi in Bengal.

items.f: 1. I live in the desert. 2. I have long eyelashes and wide, soft feet. 3. My hump is full of fat.
items.b: A camel.

items.f: 1. I am a plant. 2. I have spines in place of leaves. 3. I keep water in my thick green stem.
items.b: A cactus.

items.f: 1. I am a plant who grows in a pond. 2. My leaves float. 3. Rain rolls off my waxy leaves.
items.b: A lotus.

items.f: 1. I live high in the snowy mountains of Ladakh. 2. I have thick fur and wide, furry paws. 3. I wrap my long tail round my face to sleep.
items.b: A snow leopard.

items.f: 1. I am a fish who lives on mud by the sea. 2. I hop about at low tide. 3. I can breathe through my skin.
items.b: A mudskipper.

items.f: 1. I am a tree who grows in salty mud. 2. The sea comes in and out around me. 3. My roots poke up out of the mud to get air.
items.b: A mangrove tree.

items.f: 1. I am a fish with no swim bladder. 2. I have a big, oily liver. 3. If I stop swimming, I slowly sink.
items.b: A shark.

items.f: 1. I am a seed. 2. I float on the sea for weeks. 3. I can grow into a tall tree on a far-away beach.
items.b: A coconut.

items.f: 1. I am a plant who stores water in thick, juicy leaves. 2. I open the holes in my leaves at night. 3. Many people keep me on a sunny balcony.
items.b: An aloe plant.

items.f: 1. I am a bird. 2. My family once nested on cliffs. 3. Now I nest on window ledges in cities.
items.b: A pigeon.

items.f: 1. I am an animal. 2. I sweat to keep cool on a hot day. 3. I read this card out loud.
items.b: A human, like you.

rules: Mix the cards and put them in a pile, answers facing down. Have a paper and pencil to keep score.
One player is the reader. The reader picks up the top card and reads clue 1 aloud.
The other players may make one guess each. A right guess after clue 1 wins 3 points.
If nobody is right, the reader reads clue 2. A right guess now wins 2 points.
If nobody is right, the reader reads clue 3. A right guess now wins 1 point.
If nobody is right after clue 3, nobody scores. With two players, you take turns being the reader and the guesser.
The reader turns the card over and reads the answer aloud. Then the next player becomes the reader.
When the pile is finished, add up the points. The player with the most points wins.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 12 cards. 2. Mix them and stack them, answers facing down.
flow.say: Each card is a living being. Let's see how fast you can guess who they are.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Mix them. Make a pile.

flow.do: 1. Take turns being the reader. 2. Read one clue at a time. 3. Score 3, 2 or 1 point for a right guess.
flow.say: Clue one: I have fins and gills. Who am I? Any guesses?
flow.kid: Read one clue. Let the others guess. Then read the next.

ask.q: Which clue helped you most? Why?
good: The one about the place they live.
The one about the body part, like spines or fins.

flow.parent: The hard cards are the koi fish, the mudskipper, the shark and the pigeon. When one comes up, stop and talk about how that body part suits the place.

flow.do: Add up the points. Then pick one card and talk about it.
flow.say: Which living being surprised you most? What was suited to their place?
flow.kid: Count your points. Which card surprised you?

check.q: A shark has no swim bladder. What happens if she stops swimming?
options: She floats up to the top
She stays still in the middle
check.why: A shark's body is a little heavier than water. Without a bag of gas to hold her up, she slowly sinks if she stops swimming. Her oily liver helps a little, but not enough.

games.title: Air In, Air Out: a moving game
games.context: This is a moving game. One player calls out a card, and everyone moves like a fish or a camel. It helps the body remember what a swim bladder, fins and a camel's adaptations do.

printables.title: 12 call cards to cut out, with the move on the back

items.f: Air in!
items.b: Your swim bladder fills up. Rise up tall on your toes.

items.f: Air out!
items.b: Your swim bladder gets smaller. Sink down into a crouch.

items.f: Tail fin!
items.b: Wiggle your bottom from side to side and move two steps forward.

items.f: Side fins!
items.b: Hold your arms out like side fins and turn round slowly.

items.f: Back fin!
items.b: Stand still with one hand on top of your head. Do not wobble.

items.f: Shark!
items.b: A shark has no swim bladder. Keep marching on the spot until the next card, or you sink to a crouch.

items.f: Hover!
items.b: Your swim bladder is just right. Stay perfectly still, halfway down.

items.f: Sandstorm!
items.b: You are a camel now. Shut your eyes and pinch your nose for a count of three.

items.f: Hot sand!
items.b: You are a camel. Kneel down on your knee pads.

items.f: Out of the water!
items.b: Your gills stick together. Freeze, then flop on the floor like a fish.

items.f: Mudskipper!
items.b: Hop like a mudskipper on the mud, three hops.

items.f: Back in the water!
items.b: Stand up and swim with your arms. You can breathe again.

rules: Clear a space on the floor, away from sharp corners.
One player is the caller. The caller mixes the cards and reads the front of one card aloud.
Everyone else does the move on the back. If you are not sure, the caller reads the back aloud.
Anyone who does a different move sits out for one card.
After 6 cards, a new player becomes the caller. When the cards run out, mix them and use them again.
Play until everyone has had a turn as the caller.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 12 cards. 2. Clear a space. 3. Read every card aloud once together.
flow.say: Let's learn the moves first. When I say air in, what do you do?
flow.kid: Learn the moves. Air in means stand tall.

flow.do: Play the game. Take turns being the caller.
flow.say: Air in! Air out! Hover! Shark!
flow.kid: Listen to the caller. Do the move fast!
flow.parent: Call the cards quickly once the moves are known. Mix fish and camel cards so children have to think.

flow.do: Sit down and ask one question.

flow.kid: Why did the shark keep moving?

ask.q: Why did the shark have to keep moving?
good: Because a shark has no swim bladder.

experiments.title: The Bottle Fish: how much air stops a heavy body sinking?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make a 'fish' from a bottle with coins inside. The coins make it heavier than water, like a real fish's bones and muscles. Then you find out how much air the bottle needs inside to float.
experiments.question: A bottle with coins inside sinks when it is full of water. How many spoons of air does it need before it floats?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the bottle need a lot of air to float, about half a bottle, or only a little? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same bottle, the same coins and the same bucket each time. The only change is how much air is inside. We test each amount twice, because a bubble stuck on the outside can fool us once.
results_table: Spoons of water poured out (spoons of air in)

materials.item: a clear plastic bottle with a cap, about 500 ml, with the label taken off
5 one-rupee coins, which just fit through most bottle mouths. If they do not fit, use small stones from a flower pot, or small steel nuts.
a bucket, filled with water nearly to the top
a tablespoon (about 15 ml)
an old towel, for spills

experiments.safety: Wipe up spilled water at once, so nobody slips. Never leave a baby or a small child alone near a bucket of water.

schedule.what: Make the bottle fish and fill the bottle under water. Swap water for air one spoon at a time, and test if it sinks or floats.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the bottle fish on the bottom of the bucket, and again floating at the top. Write how many spoons of air it needed.

flow.do: 1. Put the coins into the empty bottle. 2. Hold the bottle under the water in the bucket. 3. Let it fill right to the top, until no more bubbles come out. 4. Close the cap under the water.
flow.say: This bottle is our fish. The coins are like a fish's bones and muscles. Bones and muscles are heavier than water.
flow.kid: Put the coins in the bottle. Fill it under the water. Close the cap.
flow.parent: Filling the bottle under water gets every bubble out. Even one big bubble can make it float, so fill it slowly.

flow.do: Hold the closed bottle in the middle of the water. Let go and watch.
flow.say: Let go. Does our fish sink or float?
flow.kid: Let go. Does the bottle sink or float?
flow.parent: The bottle must sink to the bottom. If it floats, open it, add one more coin or stone, and fill it under water again.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess and to say why. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will swap some water for air, one spoon at a time. How many spoons until it floats? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: We will add air, one spoon at a time. How many spoons to float? Why?

flow.do: 1. Take the bottle out and open it. 2. Pour one tablespoon of water out of the bottle. 3. Close the cap. 4. Put the bottle under the water and let go. 5. Write sinks or floats in the table. 6. Test it once more.
flow.say: One spoon of water out means one spoon of air in. Now let go. Sink or float?
flow.kid: Pour out one spoon of water. Close it. Let go. Sink or float?
flow.parent: Pour slowly from the bottle into the spoon, over the bucket. Each time, push the bottle to the middle of the water before you let go. Many 500 ml bottles with five coins float after two to four tablespoons. Tilt the bottle slowly to fill the spoon, then stand the bottle straight.

flow.do: 1. Keep going, one spoon at a time, until the bottle floats. 2. Then pour out three more spoons and test again. 3. Look at how high it floats now.
flow.say: How many spoons did it need? Now let's add even more air. Does it float higher?
flow.kid: Keep going until it floats. Then pour out three more spoons.

ask.q: How many spoons of air did the bottle need to float?
good: Only two or three spoons.
Just a little air, much less than half the bottle.

flow.do: Ask your child three things. What do you think? What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.say: The bottle had coins and lots of water inside, but only a little air. Why did a little air help so much?
flow.kid: What did you see? Why did a little air help?

ask.q: Why did a little air make the heavy bottle float?
good: Air is very light, so the bottle got lighter.
The air took the place of some heavy water.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses the result. With no air it sank, and with a little air it floated. Air is much lighter than water. Swapping a little water for air made the whole bottle light enough to float. Many fish have a bag of gas inside like this, called a swim bladder.

check.q: Many fish have a small bag of gas inside, called a swim bladder. What does it do for the fish?
options: It helps the fish see in the dark
It stops the fish from sinking
It makes the fish's fins grow
check.why: Like the air in your bottle, the swim bladder makes the fish as light as the water around her. Then she can stay at one depth without sinking.

experiments.title: Wrinkly Fingers: do they grip wet things better?
experiments.context: In this experiment you test a question that scientists still argue about. When your hands stay in water, your fingertips go wrinkly. Some scientists think this helps us grip wet things, like treads on a tyre. You find out for yourself.
experiments.question: Can you move wet marbles from one bowl to another faster with wrinkly fingertips than with smooth ones?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will wrinkly fingers be faster, slower or the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same marbles, the same bowls and the same hand each time, for 30 seconds each. We practise twice first, because people get faster with practice, and we don't want practice to fool us.

materials.item: 15 glass marbles, or 15 small steel nuts
2 bowls, one with water in it
a basin or a big bowl of warm water, as warm as a bath
a phone or clock to time 30 seconds
a towel

experiments.safety: A grown-up checks that the soaking water is only bath-warm, never hot.

schedule.what: Practise and test with smooth fingers. Soak your hand until the fingertips wrinkle. Test again.

experiments.record: Write the number of marbles moved with smooth fingers and with wrinkly fingers. Draw a wrinkly fingertip.

flow.do: 1. Put the marbles in the bowl of water. 2. Put the empty bowl next to it. 3. Your child uses one thumb and one finger to move marbles, one at a time, for 30 seconds. 4. Do this twice to practise.
flow.say: Pick up one marble at a time with your thumb and one finger. Move it to the empty bowl. Ready? Go!
flow.kid: Move the wet marbles, one by one. Go!
flow.parent: The two practice tries are only for getting used to it. Do not count them.

flow.do: Now do one real test with smooth fingers. Count the marbles moved in 30 seconds. Write the number down.
flow.say: This is the real test. Thirty seconds. Go!
flow.kid: Real test. Move as many as you can!

flow.do: Ask your child to guess and to say why.
flow.say: Soon your fingertips will go wrinkly. Will you be faster, slower or the same? Why?
flow.kid: Will wrinkly fingers be faster? Why do you think so?

flow.do: 1. Check the warm water with your own hand first. 2. Your child soaks the same hand in it until the fingertips are wrinkly. 3. This takes about 5 to 10 minutes. 4. Read the story or tell jokes while you wait.
flow.say: Let's look at your fingers every few minutes. Are they wrinkly yet?
flow.kid: Soak your hand. Watch your fingertips go wrinkly.
flow.parent: Your body makes your fingertips wrinkle, using its nerves. It is not just skin soaking up water. Doctors know this because fingers with a damaged nerve do not wrinkle.

flow.do: Move the marbles back. Test again for 30 seconds with the wrinkly hand. Write the number down.
flow.say: Same hand, same marbles. Thirty seconds. Go!
flow.kid: Test again with wrinkly fingers. Go!
flow.parent: Wrinkles fade after a few minutes in the air, so start this test straight away.

flow.do: Compare the two numbers. Ask your child what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Were your wrinkly fingers faster? Scientists have found different answers. What did you find?
flow.kid: Which was faster? What do you think wrinkles are for?

good: My wrinkly fingers moved more marbles.
They were about the same.
One test is not enough to be sure.

flow.parent: Any result is a real result. In a test in 2013, wrinkled fingers moved wet things faster. In a test in 2014, they did not help. A strong answer says what happened, and that more tests, with more people, would help to decide.

check.q: Two scientists did the wrinkly finger test and got different answers. What should scientists do next?
options: Pick the answer they like best
Do more careful tests with more people
check.why: When tests disagree, scientists do more tests, carefully, with more people. That is how they find out which answer holds up.

activities.title: The Paintbrush Gill: why a fish needs water
activities.context: In this activity you dip a soft paintbrush in water and lift it out. The brush hairs behave like the thin flaps of a fish's gills.

materials.item: a soft paintbrush, or a make-up brush, or a bunch of thin threads tied at one end
a glass of water

schedule.what: Look at the dry brush. Dip it in water. Lift it out. Compare.

activities.record: Draw the brush in the water and out of the water.

flow.do: Look at the dry brush closely with your child.
flow.say: Look at all these thin hairs. A fish's gills are made of many thin flaps, a bit like these.
flow.kid: Look at the brush hairs. Gills have thin flaps like these.

flow.do: 1. Hold the brush in the glass of water. 2. Gently swish it. 3. Look at the hairs from the side of the glass.
flow.say: What do the hairs do in the water?
flow.kid: Swish the brush in the water. Look at the hairs.

ask.q: What happened to the hairs in the water?
good: They spread out.
They floated apart, each one on its own.

flow.do: Lift the brush out of the water and look again.
flow.say: Now what happens to the hairs out of the water? What would happen to a fish's gills in air?
flow.kid: Lift it out. What happened to the hairs?

ask.q: Why can't most fish breathe in air?
good: Their gills stick together, like the hairs.
The flaps clump, so there is no room for air to reach them.

flow.parent: In water, the gill flaps spread apart, so lots of their surface touches the water and takes in oxygen. In air, they stick together into a clump and dry out. That is why most fish cannot breathe for long out of water, even though air has more oxygen than water.

check.q: Out of water, the brush hairs stuck together. What happens to a fish's gills in air?
options: They stick together and dry out
check.why: Gill flaps need water to hold them apart. In air they stick together, so only a little of them can take in oxygen.

activities.title: Camel Close-up: find six desert adaptations
activities.context: In this activity you look closely at a photo of a camel and find six parts of her body that help her in the desert. Then you try some of them with your own body.

materials.item: a photo of a camel close up, on a phone or in a book
paper and colour pencils

schedule.what: Find six adaptations in a camel photo. Draw and label them. Try a few with your body.

activities.record: A drawing of a camel with six labels.

flow.do: 1. Look at the camel photo together. 2. Find the hump, the eyelashes, the nostrils, the fur on the back, the knee pads and the feet.
flow.say: Let's be detectives. Can you find six parts of this camel that help her in the desert?
flow.kid: Find six desert parts on the camel. Point to each one.

flow.do: For each part, ask your child what problem of the desert it helps with.
flow.say: What is the hump for? Why do you think her eyelashes are so long?
flow.kid: What does each part help with? Say it out loud.

ask.q: Which desert problem do the long eyelashes help with?
good: Sand blowing in her eyes.
The sandstorm.

flow.parent: Hump: a store of fat for days with little food. Eyelashes: keep blowing sand out. Nostrils: close to slits in a sandstorm. Back fur: keeps the sun's heat off her skin. Knee and chest pads: let her kneel on hot sand. Wide feet: spread out so she does not sink into soft sand.

flow.do: 1. Your child tries to close their nostrils without using their fingers (most people cannot, but a camel can). 2. Then they draw the camel and label the six parts. Your child can say the labels and a grown-up writes them.
flow.say: Can you close your nose without your fingers, like a camel? It is hard! Try it, then draw the camel.
flow.kid: Try to close your nose, no fingers. Then draw the camel.

check.q: What does a camel do with her nostrils in a sandstorm?
options: She closes them to thin slits
check.why: Closed nostrils keep the blowing sand out of her nose, so she can still breathe through the thin slits.

activities.title: Dry Home or Wet Home? Read a plant's leaves
activities.context: In this activity you look at plants in your home, on your balcony or in the kitchen. From their leaves and stems, you guess whether each plant's family comes from a dry place or a wet place.

materials.item: 3 or 4 plants or leaves, such as aloe vera, a money plant, a cactus, tulsi or curry leaves. If you have none, use photos.
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Look at, feel and compare the leaves. Guess each plant's home. Check the answers.

activities.record: Draw each leaf. Write 'dry home' or 'wet home' under each one.

flow.do: Put the plants or leaves side by side. Let your child look at and gently feel each one.
flow.say: Feel each leaf. Is it thick or thin? Big or small? Waxy or soft?
flow.kid: Feel each leaf. Thick or thin? Waxy or soft?

flow.do: Ask your child to guess which plants come from dry places and which from wet places, and why.
flow.say: Which of these do you think comes from a dry place? What makes you think so?
flow.kid: Which plant comes from a dry place? Why?

ask.q: Why might a plant from a dry place have thick leaves?
good: To keep water inside.
So the water does not dry out.

flow.do: Tell your child the answers and compare with the guesses.
flow.say: Aloe and cactus come from dry places. The money plant comes from rainforests. Were you right? What do you think about the others?
flow.kid: Check your guesses. How many were right?
flow.parent: Aloe vera probably comes from dry lands in Arabia. Most cactus plants come from dry parts of the Americas. The money plant grew wild in a rainforest on an island in the Pacific Ocean, climbing up trees. Tulsi and curry leaves are from India. They are fine to guess about, and a guess with a reason is a good answer.

check.q: A plant has very thick, juicy leaves. Where does the plant's family most likely come from?
check.why: Thick, juicy leaves store water. That helps a plant through long dry days, so this plant's family most likely comes from a dry place.

activities.title: Fish at the Market (if your family buys whole fish)
activities.context: In this activity you look closely at a whole fish from the market or the kitchen. You count her fins, look at her gills and feel her scales.

materials.item: a whole fish, such as a mathi or rohu, bought for cooking, or a clear photo of a whole fish
a plate

schedule.what: Count the fins, look at the gills and feel the scales of a whole fish.

activities.record: Draw the fish with every fin, and write how many fins you counted.

flow.do: Put the fish on a plate. Count the fins together: back, tail, two at the sides near the head, two underneath and one near the tail underneath. A rohu or mathi has seven. Other fish can have a different number.
flow.say: Let's count every fin. Point to each one as you count.
flow.kid: Count every fin on the fish.

flow.do: Lift the flap behind the eye and show your child the gills.
flow.say: These red, feathery parts are the gills. This is how the fish took oxygen from the water.
flow.kid: Look under the flap. Those red parts are gills.

flow.do: Let your child gently feel the scales from head to tail, then tail to head. Wash hands after.
flow.say: Feel the scales from head to tail. Now the other way. Which way is smoother? Why might that help a fish?
flow.kid: Feel the scales both ways. Which way is smooth?

ask.q: Why might the scales be smooth from head to tail?
good: So the fish slides forward through the water.
Because the fish swims head first.

check.q: What are the red, feathery parts under the flap behind a fish's eye?
check.why: These are the gills. Water flows over them and they take oxygen out of the water.

projects.title: A Camel and a Fish from Waste
projects.context: In this two-day project you make a model camel and a model fish from things you would throw away. On each model you label the adaptations, and on day 2 your fish model goes in the water.

materials.item: an empty small box or a toilet paper roll, for the camel's body
an old newspaper, scrunched up, for the hump
4 used ice cream sticks or rolled-up newspaper, for the camel's legs
the bottle fish from the Bottle Fish experiment, or a small plastic bottle with a cap
cardboard from an old box, for fins
sticky tape, glue, scissors and colour pencils

schedule.what: Make the camel. Add a hump, long legs and wide paper feet. Label the four parts.
Tape cardboard fins onto the bottle fish. Label the fins. Float the bottle and see how it sits in the water.

projects.record: The two models, each with labels, and a photo or drawing of the fish floating.

flow.do: 1. Tape the legs to the box. 2. Tape a ball of newspaper on top as the hump. 3. Cut wide, round paper feet. 4. Draw long eyelashes. 5. Write a small label for each part.
flow.say: What does our camel need for the desert? Let's give her every part we learned about.
flow.kid: Build the camel. Add a hump, long legs and wide feet. Label them.

flow.do: 1. Cut a tail fin, a back fin and two side fins from cardboard. 2. Cover each with sticky tape so water does not soak it. 3. Tape them onto the bottle fish. 4. Label each fin.
flow.say: Where do the fins go on a real fish? What does each one do?
flow.kid: Tape fins on your bottle fish. Label each fin.

flow.do: Float the bottle fish, with the amount of air that made the bottle float, in a bucket of water. Push it gently and watch.
flow.say: Which way does it float? Push it gently. Do the fins change how it moves?
flow.kid: Float your fish. Push it gently. Watch the fins.

ask.q: Which part of your camel would be no use to the fish? Why?
good: The wide feet, because the fish never walks on sand.
The hump, because the fish lives in water.

check.q: Why did you give the camel wide feet?
options: So she does not sink into soft sand
check.why: Wide feet spread a camel's weight over more sand, so she sinks in less.

challenges.title: Make the Bottle Fish Hover
challenges.context: This is a making challenge. In the Bottle Fish experiment, the bottle either sank to the bottom or floated at the top. A real fish with a swim bladder can hang still in the middle of the water. Can you make your bottle do that?
challenges.problem: Make your bottle fish hang under the water, not floating on top and not lying on the bottom, or sink very slowly, for a count of ten.
constraints: Use the same bottle and coins as before.
You may add or take away water, coins or small stones.
You may not hold the bottle once you let go.
materials: the bottle fish from the Bottle Fish experiment
a few extra coins or small stones
a small plastic bag and a rubber band
general: Start with a bottle that only just floats. Then add water back a teaspoon at a time, so the change is very small.
Add one small stone or coin at a time.
Use a smaller bottle, where one teaspoon makes a bigger difference.
creative: Tie a small plastic bag with a little air in it to the outside, like a swim bladder you can change.
Use a soft plastic bottle that only just floats. Squeeze it gently, and it sinks. Let go, and it rises. A fish changes the size of her swim bladder in a similar way, by adding gas or letting it out.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own hovering fish. Then tell someone at home how much air it needed, and why a little more made it float.

flow.do: Read the challenge. Remind your child how the bottle sank with no air and floated with a little air.
flow.say: Our fish sank, then floated. Can you make it hang in the middle of the water, like a real fish?
flow.kid: Can you make the bottle hang in the middle?

flow.do: Your child tries ideas and tests each one. Let them try, fail and change the plan.
flow.say: What could you change? A little more water? One more coin? Try it.
flow.kid: Try one change. Did it hover? Try again.
flow.parent: Hanging perfectly still is very hard. Sinking very slowly, or floating just under the top, counts as a win. Help only if your child is stuck after a few tries.

flow.do: Test the best try for a count of ten. Talk about why it was so hard.
flow.say: Count to ten. Why was it so hard to get just right?
flow.kid: Count to ten. Why was it hard?

ask.q: Why is it hard to make the bottle hover?
good: A tiny bit too much air and it floats.
A tiny bit too little and it sinks.

check.q: A fish wants to go a little deeper. What can she do with her swim bladder?
options: Let a little gas out of it
check.why: With less gas in her swim bladder, the fish is a little heavier than the water, so she sinks a little. To rise, she adds gas.

opts: A part of a body, or a way of behaving, that helps a living being live in their place
A new home for an animal
quiz.why: An adaptation helps a living being live in their habitat, like a camel's wide feet on sand.

quiz.p: Which fin pushes a fish forward through the water?
quiz.why: The tail fin pushes the water back, and the water pushes the fish forward. If you picked the back fin, that one keeps her from rolling over.

quiz.p: A fish is taken out of water. Why can't she breathe for long?
opts: There is no oxygen in air
Her gills stick together and dry out
quiz.why: Air has plenty of oxygen. But out of water, the thin gill flaps stick together, like the paintbrush hairs, so the fish cannot take enough oxygen in.

quiz.p: In the Bottle Fish test, the bottle full of coins and water sank. What made it float?
opts: Swapping a little water for air
quiz.why: Air is much lighter than water. A few spoons of air in place of water made the whole bottle light enough to float.

quiz.p: Many fish have a bag of gas inside their bodies. What is it called?
quiz.why: The swim bladder holds gas. It stops a fish from sinking, like the air in your bottle fish.

quiz.p: What is a camel's hump mostly made of?
quiz.why: The hump is a store of fat. Many people think it holds water, but it does not. When a camel has little food, the hump shrinks.

quiz.p: Why does a camel have two rows of long eyelashes?
opts: To keep blowing sand out of her eyes
quiz.why: In the desert, the wind blows sand. Long eyelashes help keep it out of her eyes.

quiz.p: Why does a camel have thick fur on her back in the hot desert?
opts: It keeps the sun's heat off her skin
quiz.why: The fur keeps the sun's heat away from her skin in the day, and keeps her warm on cold desert nights. Deep in the fur, near her skin, it stays much cooler than on top.

quiz.p: A cactus has spines and no flat leaves. How does that help in a dry place?
opts: Spines help the cactus lose less water than wide leaves would
quiz.why: Plants lose water through their leaves. With spines in place of wide leaves, a cactus loses much less, and keeps water in her thick stem.

quiz.p: Which plant is suited to living in a pond?
quiz.why: Lotus leaves float on the water, and rain rolls off their waxy tops. A cactus and a khejri tree are suited to dry places.

quiz.p: How did camels come to have wide feet?
opts: Each camel stretched her feet by walking on sand
Wide feet passed from parents to calves, and slowly changed over many generations
quiz.why: A calf is born with her parents' wide feet. Over thousands of generations, camels whose feet suited the sand did best, so the whole family changed.

quiz.p: Which of these is a human adaptation to hot places?
quiz.why: Humans are animals, and sweating is one of our adaptations. Sweat drying on the skin carries heat away.

items.p: Draw a line from each body part to the place where it helps.
pairs: A hump of fat and wide feet
Thick fur and wide, furry paws
items.why: Fins and gills help a fish in water. A hump and wide feet help a camel in the desert. Thick fur and wide paws help a snow leopard in snow. Floating leaves help a lotus in a pond.
items.art: Four small body-part pictures on the left and four small place pictures on the right, mixed up.

items.p: What does a fish breathe with?
items.why: Gills take oxygen out of the water. Fins are for moving and steering, and scales cover the body.

items.p: A camel's hump is full of water.
items.why: False. The hump is a store of fat. It gets smaller when the camel has little food.

items.p: Draw your bottle fish twice: once with no air, and once with a little air. Show where each one was in the bucket.
items.a: One bottle on the bottom of the bucket, and one at the top with a small air space inside.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the full bottle on the bottom and the bottle with a little air floating at the top, with the air space drawn at the top of the bottle.
items.art: Two empty buckets drawn side by side.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why did a little air make your heavy bottle float?
items.a: Air is very light. It took the place of some heavy water, so the whole bottle got light enough to float.
items.why: A strong answer says that air is much lighter than water, and uses what happened: no air, it sank, a little air, it floated.

items.p: Label the camel: hump, eyelashes, nostrils, wide feet.
a: hump: the lump on her back
eyelashes: above and below her eyes
nostrils: at the front of her nose
wide feet: at the bottom of her legs
items.why: The hump stores fat. The eyelashes keep sand out of her eyes. The nostrils close in a sandstorm. The wide feet spread out on soft sand.
items.art: A side view of a camel with four empty label lines pointing to the hump, the eyes, the nose and a foot.

items.p: Sort these plants into 'suited to a dry place' and 'suited to a wet place'.
items.why: The cactus, aloe and ker bush save water with spines, thick leaves or almost no leaves. The lotus and the mangrove tree grow in water and mud.

items.p: Three of these animals are suited to living in water. Which one is not?
items.why: A camel is suited to dry sand. A fish has fins and gills, a duck has webbed feet, and a frog can swim and breathe through damp skin.

items.p: A body part that helps a living being live in their place is called an ________.
items.why: An adaptation is a body part, or a way of behaving, that helps a living being live in their habitat.

items.p: A rohu has 1 fin on her back, 1 tail fin, 2 fins near her head, 2 fins on her belly and 1 fin near her tail underneath. How many fins is that?
items.why: 1 and 1 is 2. 2 more is 4. 2 more is 6. 1 more is 7.
items.art: A side view of a rohu fish with all seven fins shown.

items.p: Kavya and Divya live in Chennai. They are arguing about a fish and a camel.

views.says: The camel is better. She can go for days without drinking.
The fish is better. She never has to look for water at all.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason, then sees that each animal is suited to their own place.
items.why: Both are right about their animal. A camel is suited to the desert and a fish to water. Neither would be better in the other's place.

items.p: What does the fin on a fish's back do?
items.why: The back fin pushes against the water when the fish starts to roll, so she stays upright.

items.p: Remember the paintbrush in water. Why can't most fish breathe for long in air?
items.a: In water, the thin gill flaps spread apart, like the brush hairs. In air, they stick together and dry out, so the fish cannot take in enough oxygen.
items.why: A strong answer compares the gills with the brush, and says that air has oxygen but the stuck-together gills cannot take it in.

items.p: Every kind of fish dies within a few minutes out of water.
items.why: False. Mudskippers live on mangrove mud and breathe through their skin. The climbing perch, called koi in Bengal, breathes air with a special organ.

items.p: Match each desert problem to the camel part that helps with it.
items.why: Each camel part answers one problem of the desert. The eyelashes and nostrils keep out sand, the feet spread on soft sand, the hump stores food as fat, and the fur keeps out the sun's heat.

items.p: Your fingertips wrinkle when your hands stay in water. Two scientists disagree about why.

views.says: Wrinkles help us grip wet things, like the treads on a tyre. In my test, wrinkly fingers moved wet marbles faster.
In my test, wrinkly fingers were no faster. Maybe wrinkles do not help us grip at all.

items.ask: Which scientist do you agree with? Use your own Wrinkly Fingers test if you did it. What test would help decide?
items.a: A strong answer picks a side, uses evidence, and suggests a fair test with more people.
items.why: Scientists really do disagree about this. Good answers use evidence and see that more careful tests are needed.

items.p: Draw a plant for a very dry place. Give your plant one adaptation that saves water, and say what it does.
items.a: A plant with thick leaves, spines, a waxy skin or very small leaves, with a sentence about how it saves water.
items.why: A strong drawing shows one clear adaptation, such as spines in place of leaves, and explains that it helps the plant lose less water.
items.art: An empty box with a pot drawn at the bottom.

items.p: A lotus leaf floats on a pond. Rain rolls off her waxy top. Why does that help the lotus?
opts: The top of the leaf stays dry and open to the air
items.why: A dry, waxy top keeps the leaf clean and open to air and light. Water sitting on top would get in the way.

items.p: Three of these help animals stay warm in snow. Which one does not?
opts: A long tail to wrap round the face
items.why: Fins are for swimming. Thick fur, furry paws and a tail wrapped round the face all help a snow leopard keep warm.

items.p: A camel calf, her mother and her grandmother are three ________ of camels.
items.why: A generation is one step in a family. Adaptations change slowly, over very many generations.

items.p: Someone says a camel's hump is a water tank. What would you tell them, and how do we know?
items.a: The hump is fat, not water. We know because when a camel has little food for a long time, the hump gets smaller and flops over.
items.why: A strong answer says what the hump is and gives a reason, such as the hump shrinking when food is short.

items.p: A camel has 2 toes on each foot. How many toes does she have on her 4 feet?
items.why: 2 toes on each of 4 feet: 2, 4, 6, 8. That is 8 toes.
items.art: Four camel footprints in the sand, each showing two toes.

items.p: Label the fish: gills, swim bladder, tail fin, scales.
a: gills: just behind the head, under the flap
tail fin: at the back end
items.why: The gills take oxygen from the water. The swim bladder holds gas so the fish does not sink. The tail fin pushes her forward. Scales protect her skin.
items.art: A see-through drawing of a fish with four empty label lines pointing to the gills, the swim bladder, the tail and the scales.

items.p: A shark has no swim bladder. What must a shark do to stay up near the top of the sea?
items.why: Without a swim bladder, a shark is a little heavier than the water. Swimming keeps her up. Many sharks sink slowly if they stop.

worksheets.title: Thinking like a scientist about adaptations

items.p: A family of fish moves into a muddy mangrove, where the water goes away twice a day. What changes might help their family, over many generations?
items.a: Fins strong enough to move on mud, a way to breathe air or through the skin, and a way to keep water around the gills.
items.why: A strong answer picks a real problem of the place, such as no water at low tide, and gives a body change that solves it. Mudskippers have all of these.

items.p: A zoo in a very hot city wants to keep a snow leopard. The snow leopard would need a cold room all year.

views.says: People here will see a snow leopard and care about saving them in the wild.
A snow leopard is suited to cold mountains. Keeping her in a hot city is hard on her.
Maybe the zoo could show films of snow leopards in Ladakh instead.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? What does the snow leopard's body tell us?
items.a: A strong answer picks a side, uses the snow leopard's adaptations as evidence, and answers one other view.
items.why: This is a real argument zoos have. Good answers think about what the snow leopard's body is suited to, and what people gain.

items.p: Why do many scientists think a camel keeps her fat in a hump, and not all over her body?
opts: So heat can leave the rest of her body more easily
So she can float in water
So the hump can hold water
items.why: A fat layer all over would hold heat in like a blanket. With the fat in one hump, heat can leave the rest of her body. This is an idea, and scientists are not completely sure.

items.p: A camel who walks on sand all her life grows wider feet, and her calf is born with these wider feet.
items.why: False. Things a body gets by using it are not passed to the young. Calves get their feet from their parents' families, and camel feet changed over very many generations.

items.p: Draw how you made your bottle fish hang in the middle of the water, or how you would try. Label the air and the coins.
items.a: A bottle in the middle of a bucket, with a small air space at the top and coins at the bottom.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a very small air space, and explains that a tiny bit more air makes it float and a tiny bit less makes it sink.
items.art: An empty bucket of water drawn from the side.

items.p: Acanthostega lived 365 million years ago. They had legs, but also gills and a tail fin. What does this tell us about where the first legs were used?
items.a: The first legs were used in water, by animals who still breathed with gills. Walking on land came later.
items.why: A strong answer uses the evidence: an animal with gills and a tail fin lived in water, so their legs must have worked in water first.

items.p: Sort these into 'part of a human body' and 'something people make'.
items: the bigger spleen of a Bajau diver
items.why: Sweat and a bigger spleen are body adaptations, passed on in families. Shawls, boats and umbrellas are things people make to suit a place.

items.p: A submarine lets water into its tanks to sink, and pushes the water out with air to rise. Which part of a fish works in a similar way?
items.why: The swim bladder holds more or less gas, so the fish rises or sinks. The submarine's tanks and your bottle fish work in a similar way, by swapping water and air.

items.p: Which of these was a camel NOT born with?
items.why: A saddle is something people make and put on a camel. Wide feet, eyelashes and a hump are adaptations she was born with.

items.p: Mangrove trees grow ________ roots that stick up out of the mud to get air.
items.why: Mangrove mud has very little air in it, so many mangrove trees push breathing roots up into the air.

items.p: Label the cactus: spines, thick green stem, waxy skin, wide roots near the top of the soil.
a: spines: the sharp points all over
thick green stem: the fat body of the cactus, which stores water
waxy skin: the shiny outside of the stem
wide roots: spreading under the soil, near the top
items.why: Spines in place of leaves lose less water. The thick stem stores water and makes food. The waxy skin keeps water in. Wide roots near the top soak up rain quickly when it comes.
items.art: A cactus in sandy soil, cut away to show roots spreading wide just under the surface, with four empty label lines.

applications: Submarines sink and rise by letting water into tanks and pushing it out with air, much like your bottle fish and a fish's swim bladder.
Life jackets hold air or light foam to keep a person from sinking.
Farmers grow crops suited to their place: bajra in the dry Thar, and rice in wet Kerala and Bengal.
In the 1930s at Coimbatore, the plant scientist Janaki Ammal helped breed sugarcane that grows well in Indian fields.
Boat makers shape boats narrow at the front, like a fish, so they move through water more easily.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of fish live in the deep sea?
open_questions.why_open: The deep sea is huge and dark, and very little of it has been explored. Scientists find new kinds of fish there nearly every year.

open_questions.q: Why do our fingers wrinkle in water?
open_questions.why_open: Some tests say wrinkles help us grip wet things. Other tests found no help. Scientists still argue.

open_questions.q: Can living beings change fast enough as the Earth gets warmer?
open_questions.why_open: Adaptations usually change over many generations. Nobody knows how many kinds of living beings can keep up with a fast change.

open_questions.q: How did the first fish start breathing air?
open_questions.why_open: Fossils show early fish with lungs as well as gills, but how and why air-breathing began is still being worked out.

ask_kids: If you had to live in the sea, which part of your body would you want to change first?
What helps a crow sitting on a window ledge live in a city?
Why do you think a pigeon can stand on such a thin ledge?
Look at a plant on the way to the shop. Do you think their family comes from a dry place or a wet place? Why?
When you take a big breath in a swimming pool or a bucket bath, do you feel lighter? Why might that be?

jokes.a: They always have their scales ready!

jokes.a: They don't want to hit rock bottom!

jokes.j: Why did the mudskipper sit on the mud?

maths.problem: Lakshmi's bottle fish floated after 3 spoons of water were poured out. Her friend Nila's bottle floated after 5 spoons. How many more spoons did Nila's bottle need?
maths.explain: Count up from 3 to 5: 4, 5. That is 2 more. Nila's bottle may have had more coins, or been a different size.
maths.context: This is about the Bottle Fish experiment, where you swapped water for air one spoon at a time.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two results tells us whether a change, like more coins, made a difference.

maths.problem: Three rohu fish lie on the table at the market. Each rohu has 7 fins. How many fins are there in all?
maths.explain: 7 and 7 is 14. 7 more is 21. That is three groups of 7.
maths.context: This is about counting the fins of a fish, as in the Fish at the Market activity.
maths.why_maths: When every fish of one kind has the same number of fins, we can count in equal groups.

maths.problem: A picture shows 4 camels. You count 7 humps. Some camels have one hump and some have two. How many camels have two humps?
maths.answer: 3 camels have two humps, and 1 camel has one hump.
maths.explain: Every camel has at least one hump, so 4 camels give 4 humps. There are 7 humps, so 3 humps are extra. Each extra hump belongs to a two-humped camel. So 3 camels have two humps.
maths.context: This is about the two kinds of camels: one-humped camels like those in the Thar, and two-humped camels like those in Ladakh.
maths.why_maths: Reasoning step by step lets us find something we cannot count directly.

maths.problem: Your 500 ml bottle holds about 30 tablespoons of water. It floated after 3 spoons of water were poured out. Is 3 spoons more or less than half the bottle?
maths.explain: Half of 30 is 15. 3 is much less than 15. So the bottle needed only a small amount of air to float.
maths.context: This is about the Bottle Fish experiment, and how much air the bottle needed.
maths.why_maths: Comparing with half the bottle shows how small the amount of air really was.

founder: ideas/by_topic/habitats-and-adaptation.md was read. Its notes are about the ocean, the air and the monsoon, and its scientist cards (Marie Tharp, Rachel Carson, Aditi Pant, M. S. Swaminathan) are not about adaptation, so none of it was used here.
science: Fish fins: the caudal fin gives most thrust; dorsal and anal fins resist rolling; pectoral fins steer and brake. Rohu (Labeo rohita) and other carps have one dorsal, one caudal, one anal, two pectoral and two pelvic fins.
Gills: thin filaments and lamellae exchange gases with water; in air the lamellae collapse and stick together, so most fish suffocate even though air holds more oxygen.

Swim bladder: a gas-filled organ in many bony fish that sets buoyancy, so the fish is neutrally buoyant; physostomous fish such as carp gulp air, others use a gas gland. Sharks lack a swim bladder and use a large oily liver; many sink slowly if they stop swimming.

Camels (dromedaries) in the Thar: the hump is mainly fat; two rows of eyelashes and a thin third eyelid; closable nostrils; two-toed feet on a broad pad; sternal and knee callosities; thick dorsal fur that insulates against solar heat. Bactrian camels live in the Nubra Valley, Ladakh.
Fat in one hump and heat loss: a common hypothesis in physiology texts (Schmidt-Nielsen, Desert Animals, 1964), marked here as an idea.

Aloe vera uses CAM photosynthesis and opens its stomata at night. Ker (Capparis decidua) is a nearly leafless shrub of the Thar with green stems. Lotus leaves are water-repellent (the lotus effect) with stomata on the upper side. Mangroves such as Avicennia have pneumatophores. Coconuts can float at sea for weeks to months and still sprout.
Epipremnum aureum (money plant) is native to Mo'orea, French Polynesia; Aloe vera to the Arabian Peninsula; Murraya koenigii (curry leaf) to India.

Mudskippers (Periophthalmus, Boleophthalmus) breathe through the skin and the lining of the mouth and gill chambers. Anabas testudineus (climbing perch, koi in Bengali) breathes air with a labyrinth organ.

Acanthostega: Coates and Clack, Nature 1990, 'Polydactyly in the earliest known tetrapod limbs' (eight digits on the forelimb); Coates and Clack, Nature 1991, 'Fish-like gills and breathing in the earliest known tetrapod'. The 1987 Cambridge expedition to East Greenland. Alfred Romer's drying-pond idea for the origin of limbs.

Finger wrinkling needs working sympathetic nerves (Lewis and Pickering, 1935; used as a clinical nerve test). Changizi and others, 2011, Brain, Behavior and Evolution (the rain-tread idea); Kareklas, Nettle and Smulders, Biology Letters 2013 (faster with wet objects); Haseleu and others, PLOS ONE 2014 (no effect).
Ilardo and others, Cell 2018: Bajau divers have larger spleens than the neighbouring Saluan. Huerta-Sánchez and others, Nature 2014: the EPAS1 variant in Tibetans came from Denisovans.
E. K. Janaki Ammal at the Sugarcane Breeding Institute, Coimbatore, in the 1930s: hybrid sugarcanes suited to Indian conditions.
Tirukkural, chapter 50 (Knowing the Place), couplet 495. Zhuangzi, chapter 18 (Supreme Happiness), the seabird of Lu, in Burton Watson's translation.
Fish learning and memory: Brown, Animal Behaviour 2001 (crimson-spotted rainbowfish remembered an escape route for 11 months). Fish pain is debated (Sneddon and others; Key 2016).

roots.context: We have looked at fins, gills, a swim bladder, a camel's hump and a cactus's spines, and made a bottle fish float. Now we ask what being suited to a place tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your bottle fish sank when the bottle was full of coins and water. Swapping just a few spoons of water for air made the same bottle float. Air is much lighter than water, so a little air was enough to keep the heavy bottle up. A fish's small swim bladder keeps her heavy body from sinking in the same way.
deep_truth.habit: We think heavy things sink and light things float. But a body of heavy bones and muscles floats in mid-water with only a small bag of gas inside. Whether a body sinks depends on how heavy it is for its size, compared with the water around it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Bottle Fish test, the full bottle with coins sank every time. After two to four spoons of water were swapped for air, the same bottle with the same coins floated.

three.who_am_i: You are an animal suited to your place too. You sweat to cool down, and the bones in your arm come from the fin bones of fish long ago.
three.what_is_life: Living beings come in shapes that fit their homes: fins for water, wide feet for sand, spines for dry ground.
three.what_is_this_world: Each place on Earth asks different things of a body. The living beings there answer in their own ways.

roots.thread: Fish, camels, cactus plants and you belong to one very old family of life. Long ago, all of them came from the same early living beings. Over very many generations, that family spread into seas, deserts and snowy mountains, and their bodies changed to suit each place. Your arm and a fish's fin are built on the same pattern of bones. One family of life became many shapes, one for each kind of home.

teachings.source: Tirukkural 495, chapter 50 (Knowing the Place), by Thiruvalluvar
teachings.teaching: In deep water, a crocodile beats anyone who fights her. Out of the water, anyone can beat the crocodile.
teachings.link: A body's strength belongs to a body in their own place. Your bottle fish needed water to float, and a camel's wide feet help her only on sand.

teachings.source: Zhuangzi, chapter 18 (Supreme Happiness), the seabird of Lu
teachings.teaching: A seabird landed near the city of Lu. The ruler welcomed the bird with music, wine and fine meat. The bird was frightened, ate nothing and died in three days. Zhuangzi says the ruler cared for the bird the way he would care for himself, not the way a bird lives.
teachings.link: What suits one being can harm another. A fish needs water around her gills, and a camel needs dry sand under her feet.

science.text: The bones in your arm and the bones in a fish's fin come from the same ancient ancestors. Scientists see this in fossils, and in how the bones grow in a baby before birth.
Fish learn and remember. Some fish have remembered the way out of a net for almost a year. Whether fish feel pain the way we do is still argued about.

other_view.view: A body part was not made for a purpose. Over many generations, the young who happened to have useful parts lived longer and had more young. Saying 'fins are for swimming' is a short way of saying this.

how_we_found_out.story: Your arms and legs came, very long ago, from the fins of fish. But why did fins turn into legs? For many years, many scientists, such as Alfred Romer in America, thought it happened because of land. They said some fish lived in ponds that dried up. Fish with strong fins crawled over land to the next pond, and over a long time their fins became legs. In 1987, Jenny Clack, a scientist from Cambridge in England, led a team to the cold mountains of East Greenland. In the rocks they found skeletons of an animal called Acanthostega, who lived about 365 million years ago. Acanthostega had four legs, with eight fingers on each front leg. But they also had gills like a fish, and a flat tail with a fin. Their legs were too weak to walk well on land. So the first legs grew on animals who still lived in water. Legs may have helped them push through shallow, weedy water. Walking on land came later.
how_we_found_out.who: Jenny Clack, a scientist who studied fossils at the University of Cambridge, with her team; Alfred Romer, an American scientist who held the older idea
how_we_found_out.when: The expedition was in 1987, in East Greenland. The main papers came out in 1990 and 1991.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many scientists thought legs first grew so that fish could crawl over land from one drying pond to the next. Acanthostega had legs, but also gills and a tail fin, and lived in water. So legs first suited life in water.

quiz: A camel's hump is a store of fat, which she uses when food is short.
Fat is stored food, so a hungry camel's hump gets smaller.
A camel's hump is full of water, so she can walk far in a desert.
The hump is mostly fat, not water. It shrinks and flops when she has no food for long.
Every fish dies very quickly once she is out of the water.
Mudskippers hop about on mud and breathe through their skin and the inside of their mouth.
A fish breathes by taking oxygen out of the water with her gills.
Gills pull oxygen out of water, so a fish can breathe without coming up for air.
A small bag of air inside a fish helps stop her sinking.
Gas is very light, so even a little of it inside the body holds a fish up.
Legs first grew on fish so that they could walk out onto land.
An early animal with legs also had gills and a tail fin, and lived in water.
Body parts that suit a habitat pass from parents to young over many generations.
Adaptations are passed down in a family and change slowly over very many generations.
Fingers wrinkle in water so that we can grip wet things better.
In a test in 2014, wrinkled fingers did not help at all, and scientists still argue.
Humans are not animals, so people have no body parts suited to their places.
Humans are animals, and our bodies and habits are suited to our habitats too.
A cactus spine is a leaf that has changed shape to suit a dry place.
A cactus has hard, sharp leaves that changed shape, which suits a place with very little rain.
odd: Fins, gills and the swim bladder help a fish live in water; the hump helps a camel in a hot, dry place.
Cactus, khejri and camel are suited to dry places with little rain; a lotus has soft leaves for wet places.
The first three hold air, which is light and keeps them floating; a coin has no air and sinks.
Hump, fins and spines pass from parents to young; a scar comes from one life and is not passed on.
Fish and tadpoles breathe in water with gills, but a camel breathes air with lungs.
